newsitem.title: THAILAND: Margin exposure seen rising as Thai bourse falls.
newsitem.headline: Margin exposure seen rising as Thai bourse falls.

text.p: The amount of margin loans due for settlement on the Thai stock market was estimated to have reached 25 to 30 billion baht, brokers said on Friday.
They said a combination of a rapidly falling stock market and the relaxation of forced sale and margin call rules had seen exposure spiral by 10 billion baht this month alone.

Since October 1, the Thai market has been hit by foreign fund selling. By the close on Thursday it had lost 152.64 points, or 14 percent, to a three-year low of 933.00 points. It eased further on Friday and was trading at 927.07 near the close.
On September 17, margin loans in the market were estimated by analysts to total 142.1 billion baht, up from 122.3 billion baht calculated by the Bank of Thailand in June.
Of the mid-September total, margin debts due for settlement were put at 16 billion baht.

"The exposure a month ago was 16 billion, but the market was much higher then. With the index going this far below 1,000 points you can probably add 10 billion baht to the size of outstanding margin loans, " said an analyst at a leading European broker.
"The market has fallen so quickly that even if companies have been trying to force sales they haven't been able to get rid of stocks because there are so few bidders," he said.
Several finance companies carry high levels of receivable securities on their books, of which margin loans account for up to 90 percent.
Although retail clients make up the bulk of stock purchases on margin, some regional buyers also use the mechanism.

Brokers said stocks most heavily bought on margin include Krisada Mahanakorn Plc, Nava Finance and Securities Plc, Natural Park Plc, Castle Peak Holdings Plc, Finance One Plc, Hemaraj Land and Development Plc and CMIC Finance and Securities Plc.
As of last month margin purchases on the 20 most-leveraged stocks were worth 36.98 billion baht, they added.

Dongrak Bumpitak, associate in the the Stock Exchange of Thailand's examination and supervision department, said on Thursday that the recent relaxation of rules governing forced sales and margin calls would remain until the market improved.
Previous rules forcing sales, or requiring clients to increase collateral when a share price fell 15 percent, were scrapped because they had added to selling pressure in the market.

"Now they (companies that financed margin purchases) face a decision about whether to refinance their clients, but they are worried about asset quality," said Vason Thangkavivit, head of research at Pacific Finance and Securities Plc. "It really depends on the company itself and the client; their history with the company and their creditworthiness."
A 10 billion baht government fund made available on September 17 to ease margin loan burdens was over-subscribed by over 40 brokers and sub-brokers eager to borrow at preferential rates.
